sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks
domanda: A storage account named storage1 has its firewall default action set to Deny. You must permit traffic from several internet-facing locations by adding IP network rules. Which value will Azure REJECT when you attempt to add it as an IP network rule?
spiegazione: Correct: 192.168.10.0/24 falls inside the private address space defined by RFC 1918. Azure Storage IP network rules are allowed only for public internet IP addresses, and ranges reserved for private networks (addresses starting with 10, 172.16 through 172.31, and 192.168) are not accepted. Wrong - 52.239.0.0/16: this is a routable public CIDR range and is accepted. Wrong - 203.0.113.45: individual public IP addresses are explicitly supported; the documentation shows rules in the form of a single address such as 16.17.18.19. Wrong - 198.51.100.0/24: a public range expressed in valid CIDR notation, in the documented form 16.17.18.0/24, and it is not one of the unsupported /31 or /32 prefix sizes, so it is accepted. Correction: the rationale for 198.51.100.0/24 previously described the prefix as "larger than /31", which inverts prefix-length terminology; it now states the range is accepted because it is not a /31 or /32.

domanda: A member of your security operations team must be able to list and regenerate the access keys of a storage account named storage1. The user must NOT be able to modify any other property of the storage account and must not receive any Microsoft Entra ID-based access to blob data. Following the principle of least privilege, which built-in Azure role should you assign?
opzione_c: Storage Account Key Operator Service Role
spiegazione: Correct: the Storage Account Key Operator Service Role includes Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/listkeys/action and Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/regeneratekey/action, which are exactly the permissions required to view and rotate account access keys, and nothing more. Wrong - Storage Account Contributor: it does include listkeys, but it also grants Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/write, allowing the user to change any storage account property, which violates the least-privilege requirement. Wrong - Storage Blob Data Owner: this is a data-plane role that grants Microsoft Entra ID-based access to blob data; it does not grant listkeys or regeneratekey. Wrong - Reader: it can view the storage account resource but does not include listkeys/action, so the keys cannot be retrieved or regenerated.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks
domanda: Storage account storage1 has a firewall with the default action set to Deny and a single IP network rule that permits the public IP address of a virtual machine named VM1. VM1 resides in Subnet1 of VNet1 and has been reaching blob data successfully for months. After a network engineer enables the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on Subnet1, VM1 immediately begins receiving HTTP 403 errors when it calls the blob endpoint. What is the MOST likely cause?
opzione_a: Enabling the service endpoint switched the source address of the traffic to a private virtual network address, so the existing IP network rule no longer matches.
opzione_b: Enabling the service endpoint automatically regenerated the account access keys, invalidating the connection string used by VM1.
opzione_c: Enabling the service endpoint set the storage account's Public network access property to Disabled.
opzione_d: Enabling the service endpoint requires the storage account and the virtual network to be in different regions, and they are in the same region.
spiegazione: Correct: with a service endpoint enabled, traffic from the subnet stops using a public IP address and uses the private virtual network address as the source IP instead. Microsoft Learn states explicitly that IP network rules permitting traffic from those subnets no longer have an effect. The fix is to add a virtual network rule for Subnet1. Wrong - key regeneration: enabling a service endpoint is a networking operation and has no effect on account access keys; a bad key would also produce an authorization failure signature, not a firewall denial. Wrong - Public network access set to Disabled: enabling a service endpoint on a subnet does not modify the storage account's public network access setting; that is a separate, explicit configuration on the account. Wrong - different regions: the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint provides connectivity to storage accounts in the same region as the virtual network, so same-region placement is the normal, supported scenario, not an error.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks
domanda: For a general-purpose v2 storage account named storage1, an administrator sets Public network access to Disabled and creates a private endpoint in Subnet1 with the target sub-resource set to blob. Applications in Subnet1 can now read blobs successfully, but a virtual machine in Subnet1 fails to mount an Azure file share hosted in storage1 over SMB. What should you do to resolve the failure?
opzione_a: Create an additional private endpoint for storage1 and set its target sub-resource to file.
opzione_b: Add a virtual network rule for Subnet1 to the storage account firewall.
opzione_c: Enable the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on Subnet1.
opzione_d: Change Public network access to Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses.
spiegazione: Correct: a separate private endpoint is required for each storage resource you need to access. Blobs, Data Lake Storage, Files, Queues, Tables, and Static Websites are each defined as a distinct target sub-resource, so a blob private endpoint provides no connectivity to the file endpoint. Private endpoints support all protocols the account supports, including SMB. Wrong - virtual network rule: storage firewall rules only govern access through the public endpoint. With public network access disabled the public endpoint is unavailable, and a virtual network rule would neither be used nor fix file access. Wrong - Microsoft.Storage service endpoint: service endpoints reach the service's public endpoint, which is disabled on this account, so this does not restore file access. Wrong - Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses: re-opening the public endpoint would contradict the design and would still require a virtual network rule; the documented solution for the private-access design is a file-targeted private endpoint.

domanda: Following a suspected credential leak, you regenerate the primary access key (key1) of a storage account. Several partner applications that consume shared access signatures immediately start failing with authorization errors. Which type of shared access signature continues to work after an account access key is regenerated?
opzione_b: A service SAS that is associated with a stored access policy
opzione_d: A service SAS that specifies an allowed IP address range
spiegazione: Correct: a user delegation SAS is secured with Microsoft Entra credentials rather than the account key, so it is not affected by key rotation. Microsoft Learn states that rotating or regenerating access keys revokes SAS tokens generated based on that key, and that user delegation SAS tokens are the exception. Wrong - account SAS: it is signed with the account key, so regenerating that key revokes it and new tokens must be issued. Wrong - service SAS with a stored access policy: the stored access policy only centralizes constraints and revocation; the token is still signed with the account key and is therefore revoked by rotation. Wrong - service SAS with an allowed IP range: an IP constraint restricts where the token may be used but does not change how it is signed; it is still key-signed and is revoked.

domanda: A storage account named storage1 was created several years ago and has never had its keys rotated. In the Azure portal, you open Security + networking > Access keys for storage1 and find that the Set rotation reminder button is greyed out, so you cannot create a key expiration policy. What must you do first?
opzione_a: Regenerate each of the two account access keys at least once.
opzione_b: Assign yourself the Storage Account Key Operator Service Role at the subscription scope.
opzione_c: Set the AllowSharedKeyAccess property of storage1 to true.
opzione_d: Upgrade storage1 from general-purpose v1 to general-purpose v2.
spiegazione: Correct: the KeyCreationTime property records when the keys were created or last rotated, and older accounts can have a null value because it was never set. A key expiration policy cannot be created while KeyCreationTime is null, so you must rotate each key at least once. Microsoft Learn notes that if Set rotation reminder is greyed out, you need to rotate your keys. Wrong - Storage Account Key Operator Service Role: the button is greyed out because of the null KeyCreationTime, not a permissions gap; if you can see the Access keys blade you already hold listkeys. Wrong - AllowSharedKeyAccess set to true: this property controls whether Shared Key authorization is accepted for data requests; it is not a prerequisite for a key expiration policy, and the property is permissive when null or true anyway. Wrong - upgrade to general-purpose v2: key expiration policies are not gated on the account kind; the blocker is the unset KeyCreationTime.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks
domanda: Using an Azure Resource Manager template, a colleague deploys a storage account named storage1 together with one virtual network rule and two IP network rules. After the deployment completes, clients from arbitrary public IP addresses that are not listed in any rule can still read blob data in storage1. Which change will enforce the intended restriction?
opzione_a: Set the defaultAction property of the network rule set to Deny.
opzione_b: Enable the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on every subnet referenced by the rules.
opzione_c: Regenerate both account access keys for storage1.
opzione_d: Enable the exception that allows Azure services on the trusted services list to access storage1.
spiegazione: Correct: Microsoft Learn states plainly that network rules have no effect unless the default action is set to Deny. By default a storage account accepts connections from clients on any network, so the rules are inert until defaultAction is Deny. Wrong - service endpoint on subnets: service endpoints are required for virtual network rules to function, but they do nothing to block unlisted public clients while defaultAction remains Allow. Wrong - regenerate access keys: key rotation changes the credentials but does not restrict which networks may reach the public endpoint; firewall behaviour is independent of authorization. Wrong - trusted services exception: this widens access for specific Azure services rather than restricting it, and it also has no effect while the default action is Allow.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks
domanda: Contoso connects its datacenter to Azure by using ExpressRoute with Microsoft peering. On-premises servers, which use the 10.10.0.0/16 address space internally, must read blob data from a storage account whose firewall default action is Deny. What should you configure?
opzione_a: An IP network rule that contains the NAT IP addresses used for Microsoft peering.
opzione_b: An IP network rule that contains 10.10.0.0/16.
opzione_c: The Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on the GatewaySubnet of the connected virtual network.
opzione_d: The exception that allows Azure services on the trusted services list to access the storage account.
spiegazione: Correct: when you use ExpressRoute with Microsoft peering, you must identify the NAT IP addresses used for that peering, which are provided either by the service provider or by the customer, and allow those public IP addresses in the storage account's IP network rules. Wrong - 10.10.0.0/16: this is an RFC 1918 private range, and IP network rules are allowed only for public internet IP addresses; Azure rejects addresses starting with 10, 172.16-172.31, and 192.168. Wrong - service endpoint on GatewaySubnet: Microsoft Learn states that endpoints are enabled on subnets in Azure virtual networks and cannot be used for traffic from on-premises services to Azure services. Wrong - trusted services exception: that exception is for first-party Azure services operating outside your network boundary, not for a customer's on-premises servers.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks
domanda: VNet1 is deployed in the West Europe region and contains a subnet named Subnet1. A storage account named storage1 is deployed in the North Europe region. You must create a virtual network rule that grants Subnet1 access to storage1 through the storage firewall. Which service endpoint resource must you enable on Subnet1?
spiegazione: Correct: the Azure Storage cross-region service endpoint, resource name Microsoft.Storage.Global, provides connectivity to storage accounts in any region, which is what this cross-region scenario requires. Wrong - Microsoft.Storage: the standard Azure Storage service endpoint provides connectivity only to storage accounts in the same region as the virtual network, so it does not cover a North Europe account from a West Europe virtual network. Note that only one of these two endpoint types can be associated with a subnet at a time. Wrong - Microsoft.Network: this is not a service endpoint resource for Azure Storage; it is the resource provider name that identifies Azure networking services on the trusted services list. Wrong - Microsoft.AzureActiveDirectory: this tag exists only to support service endpoints for Azure Data Lake Storage Gen1 and is unrelated to securing a general-purpose storage account.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks
domanda: You plan to enable the exception named "Allow Azure services on the trusted services list to access this storage account" on a firewall-protected storage account. Which of the following are documented as trusted Azure services whose resources, when registered in the same Microsoft Entra tenant, can be granted access through this exception? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
spiegazione: Correct - Azure Backup (Microsoft.RecoveryServices): it is listed as trusted so it can run backups and restores of unmanaged disks in IaaS virtual machines; this is not required for managed disks, which Azure already manages. Correct - Azure Monitor (Microsoft.Insights): it is listed as trusted so it can write monitoring data such as resource logs and Microsoft Entra sign-in and audit logs to a secured storage account. Correct - Azure networking services (Microsoft.Network): it is listed as trusted so services such as Azure Network Watcher and Azure Traffic Manager can store and analyze network traffic logs. Wrong - Azure Cosmos DB (Microsoft.DocumentDB): it does not appear on the trusted access list for storage network security. Wrong - Azure Virtual Desktop (Microsoft.DesktopVirtualization): it does not appear on the trusted access list for storage network security.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks
domanda: As part of a design review, you must document the constraints that apply to IP network rules on an Azure Storage account. Which of the following statements are accurate? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Address ranges reserved for private networks by RFC 1918 cannot be used in an IP network rule.
opzione_b: Ranges that use a /31 or /32 prefix size are not supported and must instead be configured as individual IP address rules.
opzione_c: IPv6 address ranges can be configured as IP network rules.
opzione_d: IP network rules have no effect on requests that originate from the same Azure region as the storage account.
opzione_e: A storage account supports a maximum of 100 IP network rules.
spiegazione: Correct - RFC 1918 ranges: IP network rules are allowed only for public internet IP addresses; private ranges beginning with 10, 172.16 through 172.31, and 192.168 are rejected. Correct - /31 and /32: Microsoft Learn states that small address ranges using /31 or /32 prefix sizes are not supported and that such ranges must be configured using individual IP address rules. Correct - same-region requests: the documentation states that IP network rules cannot restrict access to clients in the same Azure region as the storage account and have no effect on same-region requests, because those services communicate using private Azure IP addresses; virtual network rules must be used instead. Wrong - IPv6: only IPv4 addresses are supported for the configuration of storage firewall rules. Wrong - 100 rules: the documented limit is 400 IP network rules per storage account, which matches the 400 virtual network rules per account limit.

domanda: To satisfy a compliance requirement, you set the AllowSharedKeyAccess property of a storage account to false. Which outcomes result from this change? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Requests that present an account SAS are denied.
opzione_b: Requests that present a service SAS are denied.
opzione_c: Requests that present a user delegation SAS to Blob Storage are still permitted.
opzione_d: Requests that are authorized with Microsoft Entra ID are denied.
opzione_e: The two account access keys are deleted from the storage account.
spiegazione: Correct - account SAS denied: an account SAS is authorized with Shared Key, so when AllowSharedKeyAccess is false the request is denied for all Azure Storage services and fails with error code 403 (Forbidden). Correct - service SAS denied: a service SAS is likewise signed with the account key and is therefore denied for all Azure Storage services. Correct - user delegation SAS permitted: a user delegation SAS is authorized with Microsoft Entra ID rather than the account key, so the request is permitted; Microsoft recommends it where Microsoft Entra authorization is otherwise unavailable. Wrong - Microsoft Entra requests denied: the entire purpose of the setting is to force clients onto Microsoft Entra ID; only secured requests authorized with Microsoft Entra ID will succeed. Wrong - keys deleted: the property only causes Azure Storage to reject requests authorized with the keys. The keys continue to exist and can still be listed or regenerated by users holding the relevant permissions.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks
domanda: A storage account named storage1 and a virtual network named VNet1 are both deployed in the West Europe region. You must allow blob access only from Subnet1 in VNet1 and from a small set of on-premises public IP addresses, and block everything else that arrives on the public endpoint. Select the appropriate option for each requirement.
opzione_a: Public network access setting on storage1: [Enabled from all networks | Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses | Disabled]
opzione_b: Service endpoint to enable on Subnet1: [Microsoft.Storage | Microsoft.Storage.Global | Microsoft.Network]
opzione_c: Maximum number of virtual network rules supported per storage account: [100 | 200 | 400]
risposta_corretta: Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses,Microsoft.Storage,400
spiegazione: Public network access: "Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses" is the setting that keeps the public endpoint reachable only for the networks, IP ranges, and resource instances you explicitly allow; in the API this corresponds to a defaultAction of Deny. "Enabled from all networks" is the permissive default and would allow the traffic you must block. "Disabled" would block the on-premises IP addresses too, because it permits traffic only through a private endpoint. Service endpoint: Microsoft.Storage is correct because it provides connectivity to storage accounts in the same region as the virtual network, and VNet1 and storage1 are both in West Europe. Microsoft.Storage.Global is the cross-region endpoint and is unnecessary here; only one of the two can be associated with a subnet. Microsoft.Network is not a storage service endpoint. Maximum virtual network rules: Microsoft Learn documents that you can add up to 400 virtual network rules per storage account; 100 and 200 are not the documented limits.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks
domanda: You must provide clients in a virtual network with private connectivity to the Azure file shares hosted in a general-purpose v2 storage account named storage1, using Azure Private Link and the default private DNS integration. Select the appropriate option for each item.
opzione_a: Target sub-resource of the private endpoint: [blob | file | dfs]
opzione_b: Recommended private DNS zone name: [privatelink.file.core.windows.net | privatelink.blob.core.windows.net | file.privatelink.core.windows.net]
opzione_c: Endpoint that clients in the virtual network should use in their connection string: [the privatelink subdomain URL | the standard storage account endpoint URL | the private endpoint IP address]
spiegazione: Target sub-resource: a separate private endpoint is required for each storage resource, and the File service maps to the target sub-resource named file. The blob sub-resource targets Blob Storage, and dfs targets Data Lake Storage; neither provides access to file shares. Private DNS zone: the documented recommended zone name for the File service is privatelink.file.core.windows.net. privatelink.blob.core.windows.net is the zone for the Blob service, and file.privatelink.core.windows.net inverts the label order and is not a valid zone name. Connection string: Microsoft Learn states that clients should use the same connection string they would use otherwise and explicitly warns not to connect using the privatelink subdomain URL. DNS resolution transparently routes the standard endpoint name to the private endpoint's IP address from inside the virtual network, and taking a dependency on a hard-coded IP address is discouraged.

domanda: Your governance team requires that the access keys of every storage account be rotated at least every 90 days, and that non-compliant accounts be reported centrally. You plan to configure a key expiration policy with the Az PowerShell module and to monitor compliance with a built-in policy definition. Select the appropriate option for each item.
opzione_a: Set-AzStorageAccount parameter used to define the policy: [-KeyExpirationPeriodInDay | -KeyRotationPeriodInDays | -KeyPolicy]
opzione_b: Prerequisite before the policy can be created on a legacy account: [Both access keys must be rotated at least once | Shared Key authorization must be disallowed | A private endpoint must exist]
opzione_c: Built-in Azure Policy definition used to report non-compliance: [Storage account keys should not be expired | Storage accounts should prevent shared key access | Storage accounts should restrict network access]
risposta_corretta: -KeyExpirationPeriodInDay,Both access keys must be rotated at least once,Storage account keys should not be expired
spiegazione: Parameter: Set-AzStorageAccount uses -KeyExpirationPeriodInDay, set to the interval in days until the key should be rotated; the same parameter is available on New-AzStorageAccount, and the Azure CLI equivalent is --key-exp-days. -KeyRotationPeriodInDays is not a valid parameter name, and KeyPolicy is the read-only property you inspect to verify the policy, not a parameter you set. Prerequisite: the KeyCreationTime property indicates when the keys were created or last rotated, and older accounts can have a null value. If KeyCreationTime is null for either key, the expiration policy cannot be created until both keys are rotated. Disallowing Shared Key and creating a private endpoint are unrelated to this prerequisite. Policy definition: "Storage account keys should not be expired" is the built-in definition documented for monitoring whether keys have been rotated within the recommended interval. "Storage accounts should prevent shared key access" governs the AllowSharedKeyAccess property instead, and "Storage accounts should restrict network access" targets firewall configuration.

sotto_argomento: Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks
domanda: A storage account named storage1 is configured as follows: the network rule set default action is Deny; a virtual network rule grants access to Subnet1 of VNet1, which has the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint enabled; and the exception that allows Azure services on the trusted services list to access the account is enabled. Evaluate each of the following statements and indicate whether it is true. 1) A virtual machine in Subnet1 that also meets the storage account's authorization requirements can read blob data in storage1. 2) Adding an IP network rule for 10.20.0.0/16 will grant access to an on-premises network that uses that address space internally. 3) An administrator working from an unlisted public IP address is blocked by the firewall when listing the containers of storage1 in the Azure portal.
opzione_a: A virtual machine in Subnet1 that also meets the storage account's authorization requirements can read blob data in storage1.
opzione_b: Adding an IP network rule for 10.20.0.0/16 will grant access to an on-premises network that uses that address space internally.
opzione_c: An administrator working from an unlisted public IP address is blocked by the firewall when listing the containers of storage1 in the Azure portal.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes: the virtual network rule for Subnet1, combined with the required Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on that subnet, permits the traffic through the firewall. Microsoft Learn is explicit that clients making requests from allowed sources must also meet the storage account's authorization requirements, which the statement stipulates, so the request succeeds. Statement 2 - No: 10.20.0.0/16 is an RFC 1918 private range and is rejected outright, since IP network rules are allowed only for public internet IP addresses. On-premises access requires the public or NAT IP addresses that the network presents to the internet. Statement 3 - No: Azure Storage firewall rules apply only to data plane operations; control plane operations are not subject to the restrictions specified in firewall rules. Listing containers from the Azure portal is performed through the control plane and succeeds unless blocked by another mechanism, whereas reading blob data from a tool such as Azure Storage Explorer would be controlled by the firewall.

domanda: An application stores a connection string that references the primary access key (key1) of a storage account named storage1. In response to a security incident, an administrator runs New-AzStorageAccountKey with -KeyName key1 against storage1. Evaluate each of the following statements and indicate whether it is true. 1) Partners that were issued an account SAS signed with key1 must be issued new SAS tokens. 2) An application that uses a user delegation SAS to read blob data in storage1 is unaffected by the operation. 3) The operation also invalidates the secondary access key (key2), so any client using key2 loses access.
opzione_a: Partners that were issued an account SAS signed with key1 must be issued new SAS tokens.
opzione_b: An application that uses a user delegation SAS to read blob data in storage1 is unaffected by the operation.
opzione_c: The operation also invalidates the secondary access key (key2), so any client using key2 loses access.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes: rotating or regenerating an access key revokes the shared access signatures that were generated based on that key. Microsoft Learn states that after access key rotation you must regenerate account and service SAS tokens to avoid disruptions to applications. Statement 2 - Yes: a user delegation SAS is secured with Microsoft Entra credentials rather than the account key, and Microsoft Learn confirms that user delegation SAS tokens aren't affected by key rotation. Statement 3 - No: a storage account is issued two independent 512-bit keys precisely so that one can be regenerated while the other continues to serve traffic. New-AzStorageAccountKey regenerates only the key named in -KeyName, which is why the documented rotation procedure moves applications to key2 before regenerating key1.

domanda: Company policy requires that the access keys of a storage account named storage1 be rotated manually every 90 days without any interruption to the application that consumes them. The application currently uses the primary access key (key1) in its connection strings, and Azure Key Vault is not in use. Arrange the four actions in the correct order to perform the documented manual key rotation procedure.
opzione_b: Update the connection strings in the application code to reference the secondary access key (key2).
opzione_c: Update the connection strings in the application code to reference the newly regenerated primary access key (key1).
spiegazione: The documented manual rotation procedure is: first update the connection strings in your application code to reference the secondary access key, which keeps the application working while key1 is replaced; then regenerate the primary access key; then update the connection strings in your code to reference the new primary access key; and finally regenerate the secondary access key in the same manner. Two keys are assigned specifically so that the application maintains access to Azure Storage throughout the process. Regenerating a key before moving the application off it would break the application, which is why option d cannot come first. Microsoft also recommends using only one of the keys across all applications at the same time, because mixing key1 in some places and key2 in others makes it impossible to rotate without an application losing access.
